'''''Salix pentandra''''', the '''bay willow''', is a species of [[willow]] native to northern [[Europe]] and northern [[Asia]].<ref name=rushforth>Rushforth, K. (1999). ''Trees of Britain and Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-220013-9}}.</ref> The scientific name refers to the male flowers having five stamens. The English name derives from the resemblance of the leaves to those of the [[bay laurel]]; other common names include bay-leaved willow and laurel willow. Its glossy leaves make it more decorative than many other willows, so it is often planted as an [[ornamental tree]].<ref name=rushforth/>

==Description==
[[Image:Salix pentandra(02).jpg|left|thumb|Leaves]]
The bay willow is a large [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] growing to {{convert|14|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall (rarely to {{convert|17|m|ft|disp=comma}}), usually growing in wet, boggy ground. The [[Leaf|leaves]] are glossy dark green, {{convert|5|–|12|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|–|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} broad, with finely serrated margins. The [[plant sexuality|dioecious]] [[flower]]s are [[catkin]]s, produced in late spring after the leaves; the male catkins are yellow, 2–5 cm long, the female catkins greenish, {{convert|1.5|–|3|cm|in|abbr=on}} long; they are pollinated by bees. The [[fruit]] is a small [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] containing numerous minute [[seed]]s embedded in white down which aids wind dispersal.<ref name=rushforth/><ref name=afm>Mitchell, A. F. (1974). ''A Field Guide to the Trees of Britain and Northern Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-212035-6}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The bay willow occurs naturally in northern Europe and northern Asia. In the British Isles it is most common in Scotland and northern England and is sometimes planted as an ornamental tree elsewhere. It grows beside rivers and streams, on marshy ground and in wet woodland.<ref name=WT>{{cite web |url=https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/trees-woods-and-wildlife/british-trees/a-z-of-british-trees/bay-willow/ |title=Bay willow |publisher=Woodland Trust |access-date=19 March 2020}}</ref> It occurs beside [[Llyn Bedydd]] in [[Wrexham County Borough]], Wales, an uncommon plant in the area.<ref name =CCW>{{cite web | url = https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263294892 | title = CCW Standing Waters SSSI Monitoring 2007-8 | author1 = A. Burgess | author2 = B. Goldsmith | author3 = T. Hatton-Ellis | author4 = M. Hughes | author5 = E. Shilland | year = 2009 | access-date = 19 March 2020 | publisher = Countryside Council for Wales}}</ref>
It has become locally [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in northern [[North America]], and is known as '''laurel willow''' there.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SAPE4|taxon=Salix pentandra|accessdate=27 October 2015}}</ref>

==Ecology==
The foliage is the food plant for the larvae of several species of moth, including ''[[Ectoedemia intimella]]'' whose larvae mine the leaves. The catkins are attractive to bees and other insects for the nectar and pollen they produce early in the year. This willow is susceptible to [[watermark disease]], which causes branches to die back, and is caused by the pathogenic bacterium ''[[Brenneria salicis]]''.<ref name=WT/>
